cards.q: What is a handle?
cards.a:
An opaque value for a system-owned object, closed by its type's own function

You never look inside a handle; you pass it back to the API. Each kind has its own closing function: `CloseHandle` for files, `DestroyWindow` for windows, `DeleteObject` for GDI objects.

cards.q: When must you call `GetLastError`?
cards.a:
Immediately after the call that failed, before any other API call

Any later API call may overwrite the thread's last error code, so read it straight away, whatever form the failure return value takes.

cards.q: Why define `NOMINMAX` before including `windows.h`?
cards.a:
Otherwise `windows.h` defines `min` and `max` macros that break `std::min`

The macros collide with `std::min`, `std::max` and `numeric_limits<T>::max()` and give baffling errors. Leaving out rarely used parts is what `WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN` does.

cards.q: Why call the W functions explicitly?
cards.a:
They take UTF-16 and keep every character; A versions can lose some

The A versions convert to UTF-16 internally anyway, and characters the legacy code page cannot represent are lost. W functions take UTF-16, not UTF-8.

cards.q: What is a surrogate pair?
cards.a:
Two UTF-16 code units that together encode a code point above U+FFFF

Code points above U+FFFF, such as emoji, do not fit in one 16-bit unit, so UTF-16 uses a high unit (0xD800-0xDBFF) and a low unit (0xDC00-0xDFFF). That is why `wcslen` gives 2 for one emoji.

cards.q: Where should a program convert between UTF-8 and UTF-16?
cards.a:
At the boundary, right where it calls a W function, keeping UTF-8 everywhere else

Keep `std::string` in UTF-8 inside the program and in files, and widen only where a W function needs UTF-16.

cards.q: What is a window class?
cards.a:
A registered description of a kind of window, with its window procedure

`RegisterClassExW` registers it once under a name, with its window procedure, cursor and background, and every window belongs to one. It is not a C++ class, and many windows can share it.
cards.lessonTitle: Windows, Classes and the Message Loop

cards.q: Why does the message loop test `GetMessageW(...) > 0`?
cards.a:
It returns 0 for `WM_QUIT` and -1 for an error; both must end the loop

Testing just "true" would keep looping on -1, because -1 is non-zero.
cards.lessonTitle: Windows, Classes and the Message Loop

cards.q: What happens if the window procedure does not call `DefWindowProcW` for unhandled messages?
cards.a:
The window loses standard behaviour such as moving, resizing and closing

`DefWindowProcW` implements the standard behaviour; without it you get a window that cannot even be moved.
cards.lessonTitle: Windows, Classes and the Message Loop

cards.q: What is the difference between `PostMessageW` and `SendMessageW`?
cards.a:
Post queues the message and returns; Send calls the procedure and waits

`SendMessageW` is a function call through the window system. From worker threads prefer Post: a Send to another thread waits for it and can deadlock.

cards.q: Why use `GET_X_LPARAM` instead of `LOWORD` for mouse positions?
cards.a:
Positions can be negative on multi-monitor setups, and it keeps the sign

`LOWORD` treats the 16 bits as unsigned, so -1 becomes 65535; `GET_X_LPARAM` keeps the sign.

cards.q: How does a window procedure find the C++ object for a window?
cards.a:
Stored with `SetWindowLongPtrW` in `WM_NCCREATE`, read with `GetWindowLongPtrW`

The pointer is passed to `CreateWindowExW`, arrives in `CREATESTRUCTW::lpCreateParams` and is stored in `GWLP_USERDATA`. The window procedure must be a free or static function, so there is no `this`.

cards.q: Why must `WM_PAINT` always call `EndPaint`?
cards.a:
It validates the area; without it `WM_PAINT` keeps coming

Pair `BeginPaint` with `EndPaint` even when you draw nothing; otherwise the area stays invalid and the program uses a whole CPU core.

cards.q: Why put the old object back before deleting a pen or brush?
cards.a:
An object still selected into a device context cannot be deleted, so it would leak

Deleting a selected object fails silently. Leaking one per paint eventually reaches the limit of 10 000 GDI objects.

cards.q: How should a program redraw when its state changes?
cards.a:
Call `InvalidateRect` on the changed area and paint in `WM_PAINT`

Several invalidations are combined into one paint, and all the drawing stays in one place, in `WM_PAINT`.

cards.q: When do you use `WM_KEYDOWN` and when `WM_CHAR`?
cards.a:
`WM_KEYDOWN` for commands tied to physical keys; `WM_CHAR` for typed text, which respects the keyboard layout

Virtual-key codes know nothing about layouts, so text built from `WM_KEYDOWN` gives a French or German user the wrong letters. `WM_CHAR` exists only because `TranslateMessage` makes it.

cards.q: How do you tell an auto-repeat from a first press?
cards.a:
Bit 30 of `lParam` is 1 if the key was already down

Bit 30 is the previous key state. Bit 31 is the transition state, which tells down (0) from up (1), not first press from repeat.

cards.q: Why must `WM_SYSKEYDOWN` messages you do not use go to `DefWindowProcW`?
cards.a:
It implements the menu keys and Alt+F4

Alt combinations and F10 arrive as system keys; swallowing them stops Alt from opening the menu and Alt+F4 from closing the window.

cards.q: Why is mouse capture needed for dragging?
cards.a:
Once the cursor leaves, the button-up can go to another window

Without capture, mouse messages go to whatever window is under the cursor. With `SetCapture`, every mouse message comes to your window even from outside it, with positions that can be negative or beyond the client size.

cards.q: What is special about `WM_MOUSEWHEEL`'s position and amount?
cards.a:
Screen coordinates, and a signed amount in `WHEEL_DELTA` (120) units or finer

Convert the position with `ScreenToClient`. Precision touchpads send small values such as 15, so accumulate the remainder rather than dividing each message by 120.

cards.q: Why handle `WM_CAPTURECHANGED`?
cards.a:
The system can take capture away, and the button-up then never arrives

An Alt+Tab or a pop-up can end the capture; ending the drag in `WM_CAPTURECHANGED` keeps the program from staying stuck in "dragging".

cards.q: Why should you not measure time by counting `WM_TIMER` messages?
cards.a:
Timers are imprecise and missed ticks are combined, so the count drifts from real time

The default resolution is about 15.6 ms, and after a busy pause a timer fires once instead of many times. Compute elapsed time from a real clock.

cards.q: What does `QueryPerformanceCounter` measure?
cards.a:
A high-resolution count since boot that never goes backwards

It has sub-microsecond resolution; divide by `QueryPerformanceFrequency` to get seconds. Milliseconds at 15.6 ms resolution is `GetTickCount64`; the UTC time of day is `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime`.

cards.q: Why store times in UTC?
cards.a:
Local time jumps with time zones and daylight saving; UTC does not, so it compares correctly

Store and compare in UTC, and convert to local time only to show it.

cards.q: What makes Ctrl+S work: the `\tCtrl+S` in the menu text or the accelerator table?
cards.a:
The accelerator table; the menu text only shows the shortcut

The text after `\t` is only shown on the right of the item. `TranslateAcceleratorW` in the message loop turns the key into the same `WM_COMMAND` as the menu item.

cards.q: Where should a program enable, disable and check menu items?
cards.a:
In `WM_INITMENUPOPUP`, just before the menu opens

Deriving the items from the program's current state each time the menu opens means they can never get out of step.

cards.q: Why should the Exit command send `WM_CLOSE` instead of destroying the window?
cards.a:
So it takes the same path as the close button, "save changes?" included

The close button sends `WM_CLOSE`; handling the question there once covers both ways of leaving.

cards.q: How does a parent window know a button was clicked?
cards.a:
It receives `WM_COMMAND` with the button's id and `BN_CLICKED`

The id is in `LOWORD(wParam)`, `BN_CLICKED` in `HIWORD(wParam)` and the control's window in `lParam`. `WM_NOTIFY` is how the newer common controls (lesson 3.05) report events.

cards.q: Why do controls need `WM_SETFONT`?
cards.a:
Otherwise they use the old System font instead of the system's message font

Controls created with `CreateWindowExW` start with the old bitmap System font; send each one the message font from `SystemParametersInfoW`.

cards.q: What gives an ordinary window Tab navigation between controls?
cards.a:
Calling `IsDialogMessageW` for each message in the message loop

`WS_TABSTOP` only marks which controls take part; `IsDialogMessageW` does the moving, in the order the controls were created. Create them in reading order.

cards.q: What does a modal dialog do to its owner, and when does `DialogBoxParamW` return?
cards.a:
It disables the owner and runs its own message loop; the call returns when `EndDialog` is called

Returning only when closed is what lets the caller test the result (`IDOK`) on the next line. A dialog that leaves the owner usable is modeless.

cards.q: How does a dialog procedure differ from a window procedure?
cards.a:
It returns `TRUE` or `FALSE` for handled, never calling `DefWindowProcW`

Returning `FALSE` lets the dialog manager do the default. It initialises in `WM_INITDIALOG`, not `WM_CREATE`, and a modal dialog is closed with `EndDialog`.

cards.q: Why should a modeless dialog's messages go through `IsDialogMessageW`?
cards.a:
Otherwise its Tab, Enter, Esc and mnemonic keyboard handling does not work

A modeless dialog uses the main message loop, so that loop must give it the keyboard handling a modal dialog's own loop does. Close it with `DestroyWindow`, not `EndDialog`.

cards.q: How does `IFileOpenDialog` report that the user cancelled?
cards.a:
`Show` returns a failed `HRESULT` equal to `HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(ERROR_CANCELLED)`

Cancelling counts as a failure, code `ERROR_CANCELLED` (1223), which is not an error to show the user. COM methods never throw C++ exceptions.

cards.q: What does `SetDefaultExtension` do?
cards.a:
Adds that extension when the user types a file name without one

A name typed with an extension is kept; the default follows the selected file type when it changes. Choosing the starting file type is `SetFileTypeIndex`.

cards.q: How is memory returned by `GetDisplayName` freed?
cards.a:
With `CoTaskMemFree`

Memory allocated by COM for you is freed with `CoTaskMemFree`. `LocalFree` belongs to `FormatMessageW`'s allocated buffer.

cards.q: What does anchoring a control to the left and right edges do?
cards.a:
It stretches the control horizontally as the window grows or shrinks

Both distances to the edges stay fixed, so the width changes with the window. Right only moves it; left only keeps it in place.

cards.q: How do you stop the user from making a window too small?
cards.a:
Set `ptMinTrackSize` in `WM_GETMINMAXINFO`

The value is the minimum window size including the frame. Fixing the size afterwards in `WM_SIZE` fights the user's drag and flickers.

cards.q: Why use `BeginDeferWindowPos` to move controls?
cards.a:
It moves them all in one step, with a single repaint

Moving twenty controls one by one repaints twenty times and flickers. `WS_CLIPCHILDREN` on the parent removes the other big source of resize flicker.

cards.q: What happens to a DPI-unaware program at 150 % scaling?
cards.a:
Windows draws it at 96 DPI and stretches it, so it looks blurry

Stretching the 96-DPI image makes text blurry. To look sharp, a program declares per-monitor awareness and scales everything itself.

cards.q: How do you scale a 10-pixel design value for the window's DPI?
cards.a:
`MulDiv(10, dpi, 96)`, always from the 96-DPI design value

96 DPI is 100 %, so 10 becomes 15 at 144 DPI. Scaling from the previous scaled value builds up rounding errors; 72 is for converting points in font sizes.

cards.q: What should a window do on `WM_DPICHANGED`?
cards.a:
Move to the suggested rectangle, re-create its fonts and lay out its controls again

The suggested rectangle keeps the window the same physical size. Windows scales the non-client area and dialogs, but your own fonts and layout are your job.

cards.q: What does the common controls manifest dependency change?
cards.a:
It loads version 6 of comctl32, which draws controls with the modern visual style

Without it, buttons and check boxes look like Windows 95. Linking is the job of `#pragma comment(lib, "comctl32.lib")`.

cards.q: How does a common control describe an event in `WM_NOTIFY`?
cards.a:
`lParam` points to an `NMHDR` holding its id and a notification code

Two numbers in `WM_COMMAND` are not enough for these events, so the structure starts with `NMHDR` and you cast to the bigger type for the code.

cards.q: What makes a virtual list view fast for huge lists?
cards.a:
It stores no items and asks only for the rows it draws

With `LVS_OWNERDATA` you only set the row count, and the control asks for each visible row's text through `LVN_GETDISPINFO`. Sorting means sorting your own vector and invalidating.

cards.q: What is the first cause of flicker and how do you stop it?
cards.a:
Background erasing before `WM_PAINT`; return 1 from `WM_ERASEBKGND`

The default `WM_ERASEBKGND` fills the area with the class background, so for a moment the window looks empty. When your paint covers everything, returning 1 says "done" without erasing.

cards.q: What does double buffering do?
cards.a:
It draws into an off-screen bitmap, then copies it to the window at once

All drawing goes to a memory DC, and one `BitBlt` copies the finished frame, so no half-drawn state is visible. The buffered-paint API does the same with a cached bitmap.

cards.q: What does `ScrollWindowEx` save?
cards.a:
It moves the drawn pixels and invalidates only the newly exposed strip

Only the strip that became visible needs painting; scroll bars themselves are set with `SetScrollInfo`.

cards.q: Which Direct2D resources must be re-created when the device is lost?
cards.a:
The render target and everything created from it, such as brushes

Those are the device-dependent resources, bitmaps included. Geometries are device-independent and survive; on `D2DERR_RECREATE_TARGET` you release the render target and its resources and let the next paint re-create them.

cards.q: Why does `SetDpi` on the render target simplify high-DPI support?
cards.a:
Drawing is then in device-independent pixels, and Direct2D scales to the monitor's DPI

One DIP is 1/96 inch, so you draw at 96-DPI sizes and Direct2D does lesson 3.04's arithmetic, without the blur of stretching.

cards.q: What does the matrix product `Rotation * Translation` mean in Direct2D?
cards.a:
Rotate first, then translate, because Direct2D multiplies row vectors from the left

With the row-vector convention `A * B` means "first A, then B", so the shape spins in place and then moves. Matrix products are not commutative.

cards.q: What is the difference between a text format and a text layout?
cards.a:
A format describes how text looks; a layout is one string laid out in a box

Like a CSS class, a format holds font, size and style; the layout has the line breaks done and every glyph positioned, so you can measure and hit-test it.

cards.q: What does "trailing" mean in a hit-test result?
cards.a:
The point is on the right half of the character

On the left half the caret goes before the character; on the right half (trailing) it goes after it.

cards.q: Why should text layouts be cached?
cards.a:
Laying text out is expensive; it only needs redoing when the text, format or box size changes

Create the layout when the text or width changes, then draw and query it as often as needed. Layouts are not GPU resources, so device loss does not affect them.

cards.q: Why convert images to 32bppPBGRA?
cards.a:
It is the pixel format Direct2D draws directly, with premultiplied alpha

It is 8-bit blue, green, red and premultiplied alpha. Files hold all kinds of formats (palettes, 24-bit, 48-bit, CMYK); the format converter turns them into the one Direct2D wants.

cards.q: What does premultiplied alpha store?
cards.a:
The colour channels already multiplied by the alpha, which makes blending and filtering correct and fast

Half-transparent red is `(128, 0, 0, 128)` premultiplied and `(255, 0, 0, 128)` straight. Storing colour and opacity separately is straight alpha.

cards.q: What is the difference between fitting and filling an image into a box?
cards.a:
Fitting shows the whole image with bars; filling covers the box and crops

Both keep the aspect ratio. Image viewers fit ("contain"); grid thumbnails often fill ("cover").

cards.q: What does error 32 mean, and what should a program do about it?
cards.a:
A sharing violation: another program has it open; retry briefly

Error 32 is `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION`. Scanners and backup tools often hold files for a moment, so a few short retries before reporting it usually succeed. "Not found" is error 2 and "access denied" is error 5.

cards.q: Why must a recursive directory search skip `.`, `..` and reparse points?
cards.a:
They lead back to the folder or up the tree, so the search never ends

`.` is the folder itself, `..` its parent, and junctions or symbolic links can point back up the tree. Following any of them makes the search revisit folders without end.

cards.q: Why use `SHGetKnownFolderPath` instead of building paths like `C:\Users\name\Documents`?
cards.a:
Known folders can be redirected or renamed; the system knows where they are

The Documents folder may be on another drive, redirected to a network share or named differently in another language, so only the system can say where it is.

cards.q: Why should a program write its own settings to `HKEY_CURRENT_USER`, not `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE`?
cards.a:
HKLM is shared by all users and needs administrator rights to write

A normal program writing to HKLM gets "access denied", as it should. The installer writes machine-wide keys once with administrator rights; the program's preferences go under `HKCU\Software\<Company>\<Program>`.

cards.q: What size do you pass to `RegSetValueExW` for a `REG_SZ` string `font`?
cards.a:
The size in bytes including the terminating null, `(font.size() + 1) * sizeof(wchar_t)`

The size is always in bytes and includes the null. Passing the character count is the most common registry bug and stores only half of a UTF-16 string.

cards.q: How do registry functions such as `RegGetValueW` report errors?
cards.a:
They return the error code (an `LSTATUS`) directly

Registry functions return the code itself, `ERROR_SUCCESS` or for example `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND`, instead of setting `GetLastError`. A missing value on first run is normal: use the default.

cards.q: Why must `CreateProcessW`'s command line be a writable buffer?
cards.a:
It may write into the buffer, and a string literal is read-only

`CreateProcessW` may write into the command line while splitting off the program name, so a literal makes it crash. Pass `commandLine.data()` of a `std::wstring`.

cards.q: How is the single argument `C:\My Folder\` written on a command line?
cards.a:
`"C:\My Folder\\"`, doubling only the backslash before the closing quote

It contains a space, so it needs quotes. Backslashes are literal except before a `"`, so only the trailing one is doubled; a lone `\"` would be read as an escaped quote and swallow the rest of the line.

cards.q: Why must the parent close its own copy of the pipe's write end after starting the child?
cards.a:
End-of-file only comes once every write handle is closed

`ReadFile` reports the end only when no write handle is left. If the parent keeps one, the loop waits forever after the child has exited.

cards.q: Why must a worker thread not call `SetWindowTextW` on the program's window?
cards.a:
A window belongs to the thread that created it; post a message instead

A window's messages are processed on the thread that created it. The worker posts a message (`PostMessageW` is safe from any thread) and the UI thread changes the window; sending to the UI thread can deadlock if it is waiting for the worker.

cards.q: A worker posts a `new`-allocated result to a window with the pointer in `lParam`. Who owns that data?
cards.a:
The receiver frees it, unless `PostMessageW` fails and the worker must

`PostMessageW` only copies the pointer value. The receiver wraps it in a `std::unique_ptr` and frees it; if posting fails because the window is gone, nobody will receive it, so the sender deletes it.

cards.q: How do two threads deadlock with locks, and what prevents it?
cards.a:
Each holds one lock and waits for the lock the other holds; always taking locks in the same order prevents it

Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1, so neither can continue. Taking several locks in one fixed order makes that cycle impossible.

cards.q: Who owns the memory passed to `SetClipboardData` after the call succeeds?
cards.a:
The clipboard; the program must not free or use it afterwards

On success the clipboard takes the memory. Only if `SetClipboardData` fails does the program free it with `GlobalFree`.
cards.lessonTitle: Clipboard, Drag and Drop and the Shell

cards.q: Which line endings does clipboard text use?
cards.a:
CRLF (`
`), by convention

Clipboard text uses CRLF by convention. A program that stores `
` converts when copying, and normalises lone ``, lone `
` and `
` when pasting, since other programs may break the convention.
cards.lessonTitle: Clipboard, Drag and Drop and the Shell

cards.q: How is the list of dropped files laid out inside an `HDROP`?
cards.a:
A `DROPFILES` header, then null-terminated paths and one extra null

It is a double-null-terminated list, the same layout as the file dialog filters and `REG_MULTI_SZ`. `DragQueryFileW` reads it for you.
cards.lessonTitle: Clipboard, Drag and Drop and the Shell

cards.q: Why must an editor remember a file's encoding and line endings?
cards.a:
So it saves the file the way it found it instead of silently converting it

A Unix file with LF endings should stay LF, and UTF-8 without a BOM should stay without one. The editor keeps both, shows them in the status bar and uses them when saving.

cards.q: How does an editor detect that a file is UTF-16 little-endian?
cards.a:
By its byte order mark `FF FE` at the start of the file

`FF FE` marks UTF-16 little-endian and `FE FF` big-endian; `EF BB BF` is the UTF-8 BOM. Without a BOM the editor checks for valid UTF-8 and otherwise assumes the legacy code page.

cards.q: Why should every "discard the document" path go through one function such as `confirmDiscard`?
cards.a:
So no way of replacing or closing the document skips the unsaved question

New, Open, a recent file, a dropped file, `WM_CLOSE` and `WM_QUERYENDSESSION` all replace or close the document. One function means none of them can lose changes without asking.

cards.q: Why is `requestedExecutionLevel level="asInvoker"` the right default in a manifest?
cards.a:
The program runs with the user's normal rights and never shows a UAC prompt when it starts

With `asInvoker` the program gets the rights of whoever started it. `requireAdministrator` shows a UAC prompt on every start, which users rightly distrust.

cards.q: Where does a per-user install put the program and its entry in Settings > Apps?
cards.a:
In `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs`, with the entry under `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall`

A per-user install needs no administrator rights, so it writes only to the user's folders and `HKEY_CURRENT_USER`. `Program Files` and HKLM are for per-machine installs.

cards.q: Why add a timestamp when code signing a program?
cards.a:
So the signature stays valid after the signing certificate expires

The timestamp proves the file was signed while the certificate was valid, so the signature keeps working after the certificate expires. SmartScreen's warning goes away only as reputation builds.

cards.q: Why does the file finder post results in batches instead of one message per file?
cards.a:
Tens of thousands of messages flood the queue and make the interface stutter; a batch every 100 ms stays smooth

The UI thread would spend its time handling a message per file. Collecting results under a lock and posting one "new results" message at most every 100 ms keeps it responsive.

cards.q: What must happen to the old worker before a new search starts?
cards.a:
It must be told to stop and be joined before the new one starts

Set the stop flag and join the old thread first (assigning a new `std::jthread` does both). Otherwise two searches could write into the same results.

cards.q: Why should the finder's Delete move files to the Recycle Bin?
cards.a:
Mass mistakes are easy in a results list, and the bin can undo them

With many selected results, one key press can remove a lot of files. Moving them to the Recycle Bin (`FOFX_RECYCLEONDELETE`) means a mistake can be undone.

cards.q: What is the difference between reserving and committing memory?
cards.a:
Reserving claims addresses only; committing backs pages with memory

A reserved range has no memory behind it, so touching it is an access violation. Committing backs pages with real memory or the page file; committed pages read as zero until written.

cards.q: You reserve 10 000 bytes with `VirtualAlloc`. Where can the reservation start, and how big is it (4 KB pages)?
cards.a:
At a multiple of 64 KB, and 12 288 bytes

Reservations start at multiples of the allocation granularity (64 KB), but their size is rounded up only to whole pages: three 4 KB pages make 12 288 bytes.

cards.q: What happens on the first access to a `PAGE_GUARD` page?
cards.a:
A one-time guard page exception; after that the page behaves with its normal protection

The first access raises `STATUS_GUARD_PAGE_VIOLATION` once, and the guard flag is cleared. Thread stacks use this to grow a page at a time.

cards.q: What size do you pass to `VirtualFree` with `MEM_RELEASE`?
cards.a:
0, together with the reservation's base address

`MEM_RELEASE` frees the whole reservation, so it takes the base address and a size of 0. Anything else fails with `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER`.

cards.q: When does `WriteConsoleW` fail even in a console program?
cards.a:
When the output is redirected to a file or pipe; use `WriteFile` then

`WriteConsoleW` writes UTF-16 straight to a console, whatever the code page, but a redirected handle is not a console. Check with `GetConsoleMode` and fall back to `WriteFile`.

cards.q: What must you call before escape sequences work in a Windows console?
cards.a:
`SetConsoleMode` with `ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING`

Virtual terminal processing is a console mode, switched on with `SetConsoleMode` on the output handle. The output code page only decides how bytes become characters.

cards.q: What does writing `\x1b[2K\r` do?
cards.a:
Erases the current line and moves the cursor to its start

`ESC[2K` erases the whole current line and `\r` returns to its first column, ready to rewrite a progress display in place.

cards.q: Why should a console control handler only set a flag?
cards.a:
It runs on a new thread, so cleanup there would race the main code

Windows calls the handler on a new thread, so cleanup there would race the main code. Setting an atomic flag lets the main loop exit cleanly; for `CTRL_CLOSE_EVENT` it must be quick.

cards.q: Where does an overlapped read get its file position from?
cards.a:
From `Offset` and `OffsetHigh` in its `OVERLAPPED`

An overlapped handle has no current position: each operation states its 64-bit offset, split into two 32-bit halves in its `OVERLAPPED`.

cards.q: `ReadFile` returns `FALSE` and `GetLastError` is `ERROR_IO_PENDING`. Did it fail?
cards.a:
No: the read was started and will complete later

`ERROR_IO_PENDING` means started, not failed; keep the buffer and `OVERLAPPED` alive until it finishes. A read that completes at once returns `TRUE` instead.

cards.q: In what order do completions come out of an I/O completion port?
cards.a:
In the order the operations finish

Reads of chunks 3, 1 and 2 may complete as 2, 3, 1, so the program keeps track of which operation each completion belongs to, for example by its offset.

cards.q: When may you free the buffer of a cancelled overlapped operation?
cards.a:
Only after its completion, with `ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED`, has arrived

A cancelled operation still completes, and until then it may write into its buffer and `OVERLAPPED`. Freeing them earlier corrupts memory.

cards.q: What does `StartServiceCtrlDispatcherW` do?
cards.a:
Connects the process to the SCM and runs the service main function

`wmain` hands control to the service control manager with it; it runs the service main function on a new thread and returns when the service stops. Installing is `sc create` or `CreateServiceW`, and the control handler is registered by the service main function.

cards.q: Why must the checkpoint increase during a long start?
cards.a:
So the SCM knows the service is making progress and has not hung

In a pending state the SCM expects the checkpoint to increase or the state to change before the wait hint runs out; otherwise it decides the service has hung.

cards.q: Which controls should a service accept while it is starting?
cards.a:
None: `dwControlsAccepted` is 0 in the start pending state

A service that is still starting cannot handle controls safely, so it accepts none until it reports `SERVICE_RUNNING`.

cards.q: How should a service show information to a user?
cards.a:
Not with windows: log it, or send it to a user-side program over a pipe or socket

Services run in session 0, separate from users' desktops, so their windows are never seen. They log to the event log or a file and talk to a user-side program.

cards.q: What does an access token contain?
cards.a:
The user's SID, the group SIDs, the privileges and the integrity level

Every process gets a copy of the token made at sign-in. Windows compares it with each object's security descriptor; passwords are never in it.

The well-known SID of the Administrators group

`S-1-5-32-544` is Administrators. LocalSystem is `S-1-5-18`, Everyone is `S-1-1-0`, and user SIDs look like `S-1-5-21-...`.

cards.q: Why can `AdjustTokenPrivileges` succeed but not enable the privilege?
cards.a:
The token does not hold that privilege at all

It returns success even when it could not enable a privilege the token never had. The only way to know is to check `GetLastError()` for `ERROR_NOT_ALL_ASSIGNED` (1300), even on success.

cards.q: Why prefer an `asInvoker` program with a small elevated helper over `requireAdministrator`?
cards.a:
Least privilege: only the few operations that need elevation run with it

The main program runs at medium integrity, and only the helper started with the `runas` verb gets the full token, after a prompt. Less code with high rights means less to go wrong.

cards.q: What must every thread do before using COM?
cards.a:
Call `CoInitializeEx` (and `CoUninitialize` when finished)

COM is initialised per thread, with an apartment model: STA for threads with windows, MTA for workers. A thread that has not called it cannot use COM.

cards.q: You receive an interface pointer from `QueryInterface`. Who calls `Release`?
cards.a:
You do, exactly once: it was already `AddRef`ed for you

Every pointer you receive from `CoCreateInstance`, `QueryInterface` or an out parameter has been `AddRef`ed for you. Forgetting `Release` leaks the object; releasing twice destroys it too early.

cards.q: What does `ComPtr::As` do?
cards.a:
It calls `QueryInterface` for another interface, into another `ComPtr`

`link.As(&file)` asks the object for `IPersistFile` and returns an `HRESULT`, `E_NOINTERFACE` if the object has none. A plain cast would skip that check.

cards.q: How do you free a string that a COM method allocated for you?
cards.a:
With the function its documentation names, usually `CoTaskMemFree`

COM memory comes from the COM allocator, so it is freed with `CoTaskMemFree`; automation `BSTR` strings use `SysFreeString`. The method's documentation says which.
